item.title: In defense of gerontocracy
item.content:encoded:
By Matthew Yglesias

In today’s hyperpolarized, hyperfactionalized political climate, one of the most reliable ways to get hosannas from every corner of the internet is to fulminate against the tyranny of America’s elderly.

Case in point: Last week, a reporter for the San Francisco Chronicle tweeted out a photo of a local town hall where residents were gathered to discuss a proposed set of new housing developments.

As one would expect, the audience members were… grayer than the average San Franciscan.

This spurred some normie YIMBY arguments about how community meetings are unrepresentative venues for political debate, as well as some ruder commentary about how old people suck and we should get rid of them.

The implication is that we live in a gerontocracy — a society where American seniors are not only clogging community meetings with their unreasonable opposition to new development but also hoarding power and opportunity in every profession and at the highest levels of government.

There are, of course, some valid concerns about the fiscal consequences of population aging and some very real cases of elected officials who have overstayed their welcome. It’s also just true that, from the C-suite to the legal profession to academia, there are more old people hanging on longer than ever.

It’s hard not to sympathize with ambitious young elected officials tired of waiting for plum congressional seats to open up or academics angry that it’s so hard to get on the tenure track these days. But it’s worth reflecting that the primary reason you see older people hanging on to prominent roles these days is entirely benign — Americans are living longer.

Share

This fact is broadly known, but I think the specific dynamics are a bit misunderstood and underrated. A recent working paper by Liran Einav and Amy Finkelstein, for example, looked at nearly three decades of data from the Medicare Current Beneficiary Survey and reached the conclusion that, while declining mortality and morbidity has increased Social Security costs by 14% per beneficiary, it has only driven up per-beneficiary Medicare costs by a much more modest 6%.

Why the mismatch between the two programs? Well, it’s because people aren’t just living longer; they are living better. The authors wrote that the increase in expected lifespan since 1992 has featured additional years that “were entirely healthy — free of physical or cognitive limitations — while the expected amount of time spent with severe health limitations fell by about 30%, reducing expected lifetime nursing-home and home-health use.”

That’s boring accounting stuff, far removed from the fun of hot takes about elderly opportunity hoarding. But it’s very relevant to how we ought to understand the gerontocracy problem. If people are living not only longer, but specifically longer in good health, then of course they are going to linger longer in leadership positions.

And, of course, not all of those people will retain their mental faculties or know when to call it.

Five members of the House of Representatives and one U.S. Senator have died in office this Congress with many cases involving members who had been ill or infirm for a while and missed the opportunity to stand down in a timely manner.

That said, congressional deaths are not exactly a new phenomenon. There was a run of about 50 years before the Civil War in which at least five members died in office in every single Congress. Congress was also much smaller back then, so the mortality rate was consistently a lot higher than in the present Congress. Further, dying members were younger, on average, than today’s dying members — but that’s because people died much younger 200 years ago.

Congressional mortality reached its peak in the 1930s and 1940s when you would routinely have over 20 members dying in a single Congress. As Slate’s Ian Prasad Philbrick wrote in April, the past few Congresses have seen a genuine uptick in deaths. But that’s because the 2010s had unusually low death rates, not because the 2020s have had unusually many.

Of course, death is a crude measure of impairment. But paired with the finding that, population-wide, people are living more unimpaired years, the fact that the congressional death rate is lower than normal, not higher, should give us some confidence that things are OK on average.

Subscribe now

Similarly, the fact that the “gerontocracy” trend isn’t limited to politics or academia but includes corporate America ought to be viewed as reassuring.

The business world is quite ruthless and competitive. Changes in corporate legal structure over the past 40 to 50 years have only made it more cutthroat. An executive team that doesn’t deliver shareholder value is liable to get fired by the board of directors. If inertia, office politics, and the old boys’ club prevent that from happening, these days, there are any number of activist equity funds eager to sweep in, buy up companies with depressed share prices, and make changes.

Nobody should be utopian about the efficiency of real-world markets, but unless you believe American finance has become cuddlier over the past generation, you ought to acknowledge that we have less reason than ever to think that for-profit companies are irrationally coddling the elderly. We have more old managers than before because it makes business sense, which is a reassuring signal about parallel trends in other fields.

Or consider the medical evidence on dementia. Due to rising life expectancy and lack of good treatments, widespread dementia is a problem that is very much still with us. But dementia rates are falling at all ages. People in their early 90s today appear to have sharper mental acuity than people who were 10 years younger in the 1980s.

If “gerontocracy” just means that a higher proportion of people live into their 70s while being in much better mental and physical shape than the septuagenarians of the past, then what is there to complain about?

We should complain about real problems

Well, of course there is plenty to complain about in life. Renters, disproportionately young, have taken it on the chin due to America’s accelerating housing shortage. By the same token (and for essentially the same reason), it has become harder for young people to buy homes.

These are real problems, and you can lay them at the feet of the elderly in the sense that the relevant policies were mostly put in place in the 1970s and the 1980s when today’s old people were around and today’s young people weren’t. But if you look at the various state-level YIMBY success stories in recent years, it’s not as if they were achieved by somehow disempowering old people.

Indeed, America’s oldest state, Maine, passed sweeping housing measures last year that have the state now exceeding its annual housing production goals. The second-oldest state, New Hampshire, also passed sweeping reforms.

But, of course, the battle for housing abundance is not yet won. People have widespread erroneous opinions about the relevant economic issues, and there is widespread irrational dislike of developers. Trying to tackle these problems directly with better arguments, new cultural products, and political organizing seems a lot more fruitful than complaining about gerontocracy and needlessly antagonizing old people.

Share

Now, it’s true that if we ameliorate the housing shortage, we will likely see people forming new households and new families at younger ages. This will lead to at least somewhat more children being born and alter the demographic trajectory of the country in a more youthful direction. But that’s to say that population aging is in part an effect of other bad policies, not that the existence of old people is bad.

Similarly, a very real problem in Congress is that the vast majority of members do not face competitive general elections. This allows infirm members to linger in office longer than they should. This is bad. But the badness is not unique to age. Democratic House nominee Darializa Avila Chevalier seems like a crazy person and is all but guaranteed to prevail in her general election due to the low levels of electoral competition, but she’s definitely young.

The tendency for political power to be controlled by low-turnout primaries, in other words, is worth fixing. It would address some legitimate concerns about “gerontocracy” while also addressing a bunch of legitimate concerns that have nothing whatsoever to do with age.

Meanwhile, though America’s frustrated young academics yearning for greater upward mobility cut a wide swath in the discourse thanks to their strong verbal skills and abundant free time, I’m not persuaded that this is a legitimate social problem. The fundamental reason that it’s hard to get a job as a historian is that there is not a lot of demand for the services of historians. This is aggravating for the specific people involved, but there are lots of fields where the number of people who would like to do the job exceeds the number of positions actually available. And there’s plenty of the opposite:

America really could use more good K-12 teachers. We could use more people with the kind of progressive values prevalent in academia working as police officers. We could use more research scientists.

For better or worse, in life, you need to find something to do that is useful to other people. Looking at declining demand for certain categories of academic work and pronouncing it gerontocracy is unhelpful.

The good news about the bad news

This all brings us back to the boring green eyeshades. The United States committed, some time ago, to meeting the financial and medical needs of its elderly population. As the older share of the total population has grown, this commitment has become increasingly burdensome.

That’s a genuine problem.

Russ Greene, a right-wing economic commentator and executive director at the Prime Mover Institute, coined the term “Total Boomer Luxury Communism“ to describe the mass redistribution of wealth from younger families and workers to the elderly. In many ways, his argument is similar to that found in Samuel Moyn’s recent book Gerontocracy in America. But as a right-wing rather than left-wing guy, he is willing to bite the bullet and say we need to cut entitlement spending.

But to a certain extent, the gerontocracy frame makes this harder rather than easier to solve.

Subscribe now

For starters, the simple fact of the matter is that the political durability of Social Security and Medicare is not a question of older people exerting raw electoral power.

These programs are broadly popular with all age groups in the electorate.

Both programs are seen as working well, with funds seen as going to largely worthy, sympathetic recipients.

Voters are also just fairly change-averse. If you proposed creating new programs on the scale of Social Security or Medicare, voters would be alarmed by the vast new spending. But these have existed for a long time and have grown slowly, so instead, the idea of cutting them alarms people.

Logically, though, if the problem is that people are living longer, then a big part of the solution should be to ask people to work longer.

I used to worry a lot about this idea because the prospect of compelling nice-but-frail old people into the labor market feels ghoulish. But understanding that “gerontocracy” is just downstream of the reality that people are living more years in perfectly good health changes the picture.

People are staying on longer as CEOs and members of Congress and professors because they are remaining sharp and healthy for longer. It’s true that not every job is as glamorous or status-rich as those positions. But that’s life.

Now, what’s true is that despite improved health, there are still many Americans in their late 60s who are genuinely infirm and unable to work.

An unfortunate reality of American life is that our disability income support programs are rather threadbare and poorly designed. What we ought to do is fix this, rather than use untargeted assistance to the elderly as a very expensive substitute. Help those in need, but acknowledge that we can ask more of able-bodied older Americans, whose physical and mental health is better than it’s ever been.

In one sense, this would make the country less of a gerontocracy in the sense that the basic fiscal bargain would be less tilted toward older people. In another, we would be more gerontocratic than ever, with more older people encouraged to hold on to their roles in the workplace and society.

Which I think mostly goes to underscore that it’s an unhelpful term.

When you watch as Lionel Messi competed credibly for the Golden Boot while LeBron James remained a prized free agent for years, both at unprecedentedly advanced ages for high-level athletes, you’re watching extraordinary human achievement, not a nefarious conspiracy of the elderly.

These star athletes are outliers, but so were their predecessors as star athletes. The curve of age and performance is shifting quite broadly, so the outliers — whether in sports or politics or business — are just somewhat more visible. And though there are some adjustments that need to be made as a result, the basic pattern is fundamentally benign and, in fact, worthy of celebration.

item.title: You don’t actually want to buy a house
item.description: The American dream... or just good marketing?
item.content:encoded:
By Jerusalem Demsas

Once a month, Matt and I do a book club episode of The Argument podcast. In an upcoming episode this month, we are reading Bowling Alone by Robert Putnam. Read along if you are interested, and please comment with any questions or ideas you would like us to explore!

As soon as I began writing publicly about housing policy, people began to ask me for real estate advice. Should I refinance my mortgage? Is it a good time to buy a condo in Northeast D.C.? Am I too young to buy a house?

I have always emphasized that I am not in the business of giving personal financial advice. But I do, unsurprisingly, have a few strongly held views.

To put it glibly, I’m anti-homeownership.

To put it slightly less glibly, I think that the bipartisan cult of homeownership — a cult that urges people to go all in on one immovable, nondiversified asset in hopes that they will be able to sell it at just the right moment to finance their retirement — is extremely irresponsible.

Share

If you want to buy a house as a matter of consumption, have at it. If I were wealthy, I would definitely find it fun to outfit a house to my exacting, idiosyncratic preferences. But so many people are invested in convincing you that it is always the correct financial decision to buy rather than rent.

David Bach, author of The Automatic Millionaire, an incredibly popular personal finance book that achieved global reach after being launched on The Oprah Winfrey Show in 2004, argued that “the most important advice I can tell you right now if you’re young is: Don’t listen to these people that tell you should [sic] rent versus buy .”

Perhaps the media’s most popular financial-advice personality is Dave Ramsey, who treats the choice to rent as a temporary state for people who are either in debt or haven’t saved up enough for a down payment.

In politics, then-President George W. Bush proclaimed that “we want everybody in America to own their own home.”

But I’m not buying it.

I probably don’t have to quote all these people because you, like me, have probably been at the receiving end of familial and public pressure to become a homeowner. And while a home is a legitimate consumption choice and sometimes a good investment, let me reiterate: It is an irresponsible public message to treat a leveraged, nondiversified, illiquid asset as the universally correct foundation for personal financial security.

My skepticism toward the cult of homeownership stems from two beliefs:

First, the best personal financial advice is to diversify your assets. And not only is a home a single asset, it is also tied closely to your employment prospects. If, for instance, there’s a local labor market shock — like the president of the United States empowering the world’s richest man to illegally fire employees of your region’s largest employer — that blow to your job opportunities is going to correlate with home prices in your area also going down.

As a result, instead of an asset that’s there for you when other things are going poorly, a home is an asset that is likely to perform poorly exactly when you need it not to.

Second is the belief is that people severely underrate the benefits of mobility in maintaining financial security. Owning a home makes it much harder to leave your region if you need to. When you lose your job — or just want a new one — homeownership acts as a drag. Two economists argued in a 2024 paper that it contributes to “lower migration to better job markets.”

Subscribe now

The cult of homeownership can have disastrous policy consequences. If politicians believe that promoting homeownership is an overriding concern, they do things like sell houses in floodplains to low-income homebuyers.

When pressed about this practice during the Biden administration, a Department of Housing and Urban Development spokesperson argued that “locking low-income homebuyers out of a great number of affordable homeownership opportunities because the homes are located in communities within flood zones not only runs contrary to the Administration’s objectives of achieving greater equity in homeownership, but prohibiting sales based on income would be comparable to sanctioning a resurgence of redlining.”

You heard that right: It is redlining not to sell a home to a first-time homebuyer in a floodplain.

Matt, who owns not one but two homes, is much less convinced of my anti-homeownership agenda. While he agrees that homes aren’t fantastic investments — and that in an ideal world, we would change a lot about American homeownership policy — he thinks that the way homeownership forces savings is reason enough to recommend it to people in general. (Allow me to reiterate that none of this is personal financial advice.)

Watch or listen wherever you get your podcasts.

item.title: Young people like journalism, just not enough to consume it
item.description: Young people are weirdly chill about the media
item.content:encoded:
By John Robert Thomason

I was recently delighted to discover that my fellow Americans do not consider me an elite.

In The Argument’s recent poll of registered voters, fielded nationally between July 20 and 26, 2026, we asked respondents who they considered elite.

Of all the groups we listed, journalists were tied as the least selected group at just 9%.

As someone entering middle age and therefore excessively concerned with what young people think of my kind, I eagerly checked the breakdown of the results by age and discovered that just 7% of the youths (18- to 29-year-olds) consider journalists to be elites.

Young people actually have a more favorable view of journalists than any other age cohort. With 57% of 18- to 29-year-olds viewing us positively, my colleagues are more popular than Democrats, Republicans, billionaires, and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. (We do, somewhat vexingly, remain less popular than college professors.)

Share

It’s hard to see young people’s attitudes as especially informed since, according to them, they simply do not read or watch the news very much — at least not without the mediation of social media.

Regular consumption of traditional news sources — by which I mean newspapers, news websites, and television — declines dramatically as you climb down the age ladder. Those under the age of 30 are less than half as likely to get regular news from TV as the general population and 8 percentage points less likely to read newspapers and news websites regularly.

Of all the traditional formats, newspapers and websites are the most used by 18- to 29-year-olds — but with just 33% of this group perusing these sources regularly, they are still distinctly unpopular parts of their news diet, on par with Elon Musk’s X. Compare that with TikTok, podcasts/YouTube, and Instagram, where 42% to 53% of young people say they get their news.

Subscribe now

Even Facebook is slightly more popular than traditional news sources, although at 36%, the youngest subgroup’s rate of regular Facebook usage is about the same as that for our age 65 and over respondents, with whom Facebook is the most popular social media news source by far.

Young people probably don’t see themselves as opting out of news consumption: Only 4% selected “none of the above” when we asked for their news sources, in line with the general population.

And, just like older voters, the 18-to-29 cohort has opinions on bias and partisanship in journalism — albeit distinct ones. While nearly half of our respondents overall think that journalists have a liberal bias, only 40% of those under 30 feel the same. This shift is primarily accounted for by a larger proportion of 18- to 29-year-olds saying that journalists are “neither more liberal nor more conservative” than any other age group.

There are a couple reasons this may be the case.

  1. Our 18- to 29-year-old respondents were 15 percentage points more liberal than our sample overall, so they may be less likely to see liberal bias than a more conservative overall population.

  2. Younger respondents, who consume primarily algorithmic media, may be working off an implicit redefinition of what a journalist actually is. After all, is a gonzo YouTuber named Reckless Ben who’s obsessed with catching an alleged Lego thief a liberal or a conservative? I can’t even venture a guess.

But as to whether or not the traditional national media are “fair and unbiased,” all age groups are split roughly 50/50. That said, there is a dramatic drop-off from the 18% of those 65 or over who believe the news can be trusted “most or all of the time” to the merely 8% of those under 45 who believe the same.

This is directionally consistent with 2025 results from Gallup, which found a 15-point gap in trust in mass media between 18- to 29-year-olds and those 65 and over — a gap that has widened dramatically since the 2001 to 2003 period when the two were at parity.

In some ways, this all confirms what we already know: We are entering a world where information delivery is increasingly fragmented and traditional gatekeeping institutions have diminished trust and influence. This has created formidable challenges for the news business and will continue to do so.

But, to the extent our survey results offer any solace, it seems like America’s young adults are approaching the field with a slightly more open mind than older Americans. And they are not particularly buying the “liberal media” narrative that the right has been pushing to discredit the profession since before they were born.

item.title: Should we bribe the NIMBYs?
item.description: Why some YIMBYs tolerate a tax on housing
item.content:encoded:
By Milan Singh

Everyone hates luxury development. But we need fancy new apartment buildings to fix the housing crisis: When rich people can move into new units, then non-rich people can move into the older homes that the rich move out of.1

Despite the truth of this, voters just do not believe that more building alone will make housing more affordable. And many politicians want the least fortunate Americans to see more obvious benefits from homebuilding.

One solution is to force developers of fancy new apartment buildings to set aside some of those homes for low- or moderate-income people. This policy is called inclusionary zoning.

Share

Starting with Montgomery County, Maryland, in the 1970s, inclusionary zoning policies have been adopted by most of America’s major cities: New York, Boston, Chicago, San Francisco, Seattle, Denver, Minneapolis, and Washington, D.C., all have some version of the policy in place.

Inclusionary zoning’s logic is simple enough: Some people will always make too little to afford market rents, and we don’t want to lock poor people — or their children — out of the benefits of living in cities and towns that have the best economic opportunities.

But economists and real estate developers counter that inclusionary zoning is functionally a tax on development, because it lowers the profit margins on building more units. That means fewer units get built overall. And, while a small number of lucky tenants get new affordable housing, overall housing costs are pushed higher than they otherwise would be, absent the inclusionary zoning requirement.

In other words, if we’re going to subsidize housing for the poor, inclusionary zoning is a really inefficient way to do it.

Just how much housing does inclusionary zoning exclude?

Figuring out exactly how much inclusionary zoning reduces housing supply growth is harder than you might think. After all, cities that impose inclusionary zoning mandates may differ from those that do not in ways that also affect the production of new housing.

Perhaps cities with inclusionary zoning are also wealthier, or more liberal, or have a higher cost of living. That makes it difficult to compare like with like and tease out the effect of inclusionary zoning alone.

But a new paper — “Inclusionary Zoning and Housing Supply: Evidence from California’s Palmer Fix” by Noah Kouchekinia, an economics Ph.D. student at the University of California, Irvine — has found a way around this challenge.

In 2009, a California court ruled that local inclusionary zoning ordinances in Los Angeles were a form of rent control rendered illegal by a 1995 state law. This made all local inclusionary zoning ordinances on rental units in the state unenforceable. In 2017, the California legislature passed a “Palmer Fix” law, which allowed localities to reimpose inclusionary zoning ordinances that were still on the books.

This allowed Kouchekinia to isolate the effects of inclusionary zoning ordinances using a difference-in-differences technique.2

The 2009 court ruling and the subsequent “Palmer Fix” provide as good a setting for difference-in-differences as you’re likely to find in the real world: Prior to 2009, some cities in California had inclusionary zoning and others did not. From 2009 to 2017, no cities in California had inclusionary zoning for rental units. Then, from 2017 onward, inclusionary zoning was “turned back on” in the cities whose ordinances came back into effect.

The next step is to find a way to measure the stringency of the inclusionary zoning ordinances. Usually, inclusionary zoning rules give developers a menu of options. For example, a developer may have a choice between setting aside 10% of units for tenants who make up to 60% of the area median income or setting aside 15% of units for tenants who make up to 80% of the area median income. Either way, the developer must forgo some share of the rent they would earn if all units were rented at market rates.

Kouchekinia assumed that developers are profit-maximizing, and he therefore measured the stringency of inclusionary zoning ordinances as the minimum percentage of market rents that they would have to forgo to be in compliance. He then estimated the effect of an increase in stringency on the supply of new housing.

He found that “for every percentage point increase in the stringency of an inclusionary zoning ordinance, the flow of new housing supply decreases by 7.6%.” Since the typical ordinance “requires a developer to forgo about 4.2% of rent,” he estimated that the typical inclusionary zoning ordinance reduces annual housing production by 31.8%.

Back-of-the-napkin math3 suggests that, from 2018 to 2024, that amounts to just over 86,000 fewer units built in the state of California because of inclusionary zoning.

Subscribe now

Kouchekinia emphasized in an email that his paper was “a work in progress” and that, while he had presented it at conferences for peer review, he has not yet released a polished version as part of a working paper series.

But his results align with prior literature on inclusionary zoning, which employs a more theoretical approach. A 2024 UC Berkeley Terner Center report simulated the effects of inclusionary zoning in Los Angeles over a 10-year time frame. It found that, as the inclusionary zoning share increases from 0% to 1%, the number of total units built decreases sharply. Then it falls more gradually and almost linearly at rates beyond that.

Another paper from Vincent Rollet at MIT built a model of supply and demand for floor space in New York City and simulated the effect of a requirement that 20% of floor space in new buildings in New York be rented at below-market prices. Rollet found that, from 2020 to 2060, the inclusionary zoning mandate would induce “the construction of 73 million sq. ft. of affordable floorspace, but lowers the total amount of floorspace in the city by 400 million sq. ft. In other words, for each sq. ft of affordable floorspace created by the policy, the overall available floorspace drops by 5.5 sq. ft.”

What happens when you secure new affordable housing units by deliberately forgoing a much larger amount of housing at market rates? Rents increase. If demand is unchanged and supply contracts, then markets clear at higher prices.

“Kouchekinia’s paper is complementary” to the prior literature, according to Chris Elmendorf, a professor at the UC Davis School of Law who studies housing policy. While “we should expect mixed effects depending on the policy specifics,” he added, the common finding is that inclusionary zoning reduces the supply of housing available to consumers overall. “There’s no such thing as a free lunch.”

We have real-world examples that appear to support the more theoretical literature as well. Portland, Maine, expanded its inclusionary zoning mandate to 25% of units in new buildings in 2020; housing production has since collapsed, and the city council is looking into rolling it back.

Portland, Oregon, adopted a similar mandate in 2017. Construction plunged until the city council voted in 2024 to expand local tax exemptions and increase financial subsidies for projects subject to the law.

Getting voters to yes (in my backyard)

Recently, Cambridge, Massachusetts (where I grew up), and New Haven, Connecticut (where I went to college), passed massive upzoning bills — a recognition in these deep-blue jurisdictions that capitalism is going to play a major role in easing their housing woes.

Last year, the Cambridge City Council passed a bill legalizing units up to six stories by right (meaning without the special permits previously required) on large-enough lots in areas with inclusionary zoning. This means that you can now put an apartment building up to 74 feet tall in places where previously only standalone low-density units were allowed. In New Haven, the Board of Alders recently passed a bill allowing for much larger and denser housing construction downtown.

Both cities have inclusionary zoning ordinances on the books. In Cambridge, 20% of floor space in a new development of 10 units or more (or at least 10,000 total square feet) must be sold or rented at below-market rates. In New Haven, at least 15% of units in new downtown developments of 10 or more units must be sold or rented at below-market rates.4

Both Burhan Azeem and Eli Sabin, the Cambridge city council member and New Haven former alder who championed their cities’ respective reforms, said that they wouldn’t have been able to build the political coalitions for their upzoning laws without those inclusionary zoning ordinances on the books.

“Without inclusionary zoning of anything, the economics would be a lot better, and we’d have a lot more housing development in total,” Azeem told me over the phone. “But that’s not the world we live in. We live in almost the opposite world, where new housing production is incredibly unpopular, where 85% of the existing buildings were noncompliant, where Massachusetts and Cambridge in particular were zoned for less density than already existed.”

“In a world where five or six votes on a nine-member council is what you need, telling someone that, in this new project, there’s going to be at least one unit that’s affordable to a teacher was a really persuasive argument to get them to see the overall benefits of the upzoning bill,” Azeem added.

Subscribe now

Sabin noted that, while he feels that skepticism of the short-term benefits of new market-rate housing is justified, inclusionary zoning might not be the most efficient way for a city to provide housing to low-income residents. That’s because if fewer units are built overall, as the literature suggests, the city government receives less in tax revenue.

“There is a counterfactual that should be considered, which is how much revenue the city would have if there hadn’t been the inclusionary zoning tax, and whether you would be able to spend that amount more efficiently to help families afford to live in the city,” he told me. “I just think that more transparency about what we’re spending and having a more honest picture of what choices are hidden within the inclusionary zoning — that would be valuable.”

Efficiency promotes equity

So far, we’ve been talking about a particular kind of inclusionary zoning ordinance: unfunded inclusionary zoning. An unfunded mandate is when the government forces you to do something but doesn’t provide any funds with which to do it. In this case, the government is demanding affordable units and expecting landlords to pay the difference between market and affordable rents.

With funded inclusionary zoning, landlords receive some sort of financial compensation for the rent they forgo on the affordable units in a building. That compensation could take many forms: In principle, the government could just write landlords a check for the difference between the market rent for a given unit and the amount tenants are paying.

In practice, the compensation usually takes the form of reduced development fees or property tax abatements — something along the lines of how Portland, Oregon, tried to fix things when its inclusionary zoning backfired.

In 2025, Washington state passed HB 1491, which set new statewide minimum density standards near transit stops. The law:

  • Imposed an inclusionary zoning requirement on new developments.

  • Required that cities with development impact fees reduce them by 50% for qualifying projects.

  • Provided a 20-year property tax abatement for new developments with affordable units.

Inclusionary zoning policies can be made less harmful, but “less bad” isn’t the same as “good idea.” Inclusionary zoning is a very kludgy and inefficient way to provide housing to those who cannot afford to pay the market price for it. A more efficient way would be to just lower the market price by flooding the city with new units.

The best way to do this would be to have no inclusionary zoning ordinances, drastically reduce zoning regulations in general, and let builders build up to the point at which housing markets clear. Then, the government would use some of the increased property tax revenues to pay for rental subsidies for low-income families — perhaps with larger subsidies allotted if a qualifying family chose to live in a high-opportunity (and commensurately higher-cost) neighborhood.

Unfortunately, we live in a second-best (or third-best or fourth-best) world. To the extent that voters and interest groups may need to be bought off to get new housing built, (funded) inclusionary zoning may be worth considering. It’s better to pad new construction with what are effectively bribes than to do no new building at all.

But we should be clear-eyed about what inclusionary zoning is: It’s a tax on new housing. And when you tax something, you end up with less of it.

Ideally, the way we would assess the effect of a policy is to randomly assign the policy to different localities. Of course, in the real world, we don’t do a random assignment of policies.

The idea behind difference-in-differences is that we can approximate randomization by comparing otherwise similar cities with and without inclusionary zoning ordinances. We can do this by confirming that the cities showed “parallel trends” on our variables of interest before one adopted the policy. That way, we can isolate any subsequent difference in outcomes as a result of the policy and not other factors.

item.title: Feminism looks better in first person
item.description: Americans agree on what feminism is. They're divided on whether it's finished its job.
item.content:encoded:
By Jerusalem Demsas

Welcome to The Closing Argument, our verdict on the news, plus everything The Argument published and appeared in this week.

The Verdict, by Jerusalem Demsas

Readers — maybe even you — love to click on stories about how young men are becoming Andrew Tate acolytes and young women are becoming misandrist shrews. Scarcely a day goes by without the commentariat debating the plight of contemporary men and women in tired, circular arguments.

Yet many polls indicate that, while voters may shy away from the label “feminist,” they have broadly positive views on the idea of equality between men and women, which raises the question: What does everyone think feminism is doing?

We asked them.

In a poll of 3,000 registered voters conducted between July 20 and 26, The Argument asked respondents “which of the following — if any — do you believe describes ‘feminism’ in practice?”

A large majority — 64% — selected “the belief that men and women should be social, political, and economic equals.” No other potential answer broke 30%.

Notably, even among Trump 2024 voters, 51% agreed with that egalitarian definition of feminism.1

For access to our full cross-tabs and analysis on all of our original issue polling become a subscriber!

Subscribe now

But when asked whether the majority of Americans and the majority of elites agreed with them, our respondents grew pessimistic.

Just 48% agreed that the majority of Americans would select the egalitarian definition of feminism, and just 28% thought the majority of elites would.

As our director of political data, Lakshya Jain, explained earlier this week, our poll generally shows a clear trend where “most people think their fellow Americans agree with them while elites disagree with them.” The feminism question complicates that pattern: There’s a 16 percentage point drop between those who personally define feminism as equality and those who think most Americans do.

That’s the single largest drop-off between personal views and majority perception in our poll, save one: the question about whether “men and women are equally suited to leadership,” where 81% personally agree but only 51% think most Americans do.

Americans’ gender egalitarianism is an underrated fact of our modern political landscape. In our earlier February poll of 3,003 registered voters, The Argument asked about a range of issues related to gender and sexuality. Normie feminist opinions repeatedly won out:

  • Only 18% agreed that women were “taking jobs that should go to men.”

  • Among respondents who thought one parent should stay home with children, 40% said it should be “whichever parent wants to stay home” and just 29% said it should be “the mother.”

Similarly, in our July polling, liberal feminism beat out explicitly hierarchical positions:

  • 81% of voters agreed that men and women are equally suited to leadership, including 74% of Trump voters.

  • Only 31% of voters thought men should be the breadwinners.

These are all positions associated with the basic achievements of feminism: Women should be eligible for the same jobs and positions of authority as men, and family roles should not be automatically assigned according to sex. Substantive egalitarian principles that feminism fought to establish are considerably more popular than the endless gender-war commentary suggests.

Before I paint too rosy a picture, the polling does show some substantive disagreement on the question of feminism — not about the value of gender egalitarianism, but instead about whether or not we have already achieved it. In our polling, men are much more likely to believe that particular gender disparities have been overcome. Women are not so sure.

This disagreement on empirical questions is no small thing. If you believe that men and women have largely already achieved equality, then any further demands by feminists can be interpreted as women seeking unfair advantage. On the other hand, if you still think there’s a lot of progress yet to be made, then feminism is merely continuing its egalitarian project — and the doubters must be hostile to true equality.

This disagreement helps explain how a country where most people think equality between the sexes is desirable has found itself continuously locked in internecine gender feuds.

Millennials, we have a problem

As a millennial feminist, I was disheartened to see that 30-to-44-year-olds had the least egalitarian perception of feminism.2

Now, I don’t want to overstate this — 59% still believe that feminism in practice is the belief that men and women should be equals — but they were also the age group most likely to say feminism means women should have more power than men (19%) and that women are superior to men (also 19%).

Nor was this a one-off result: In The Argument’s February polling on gender issues, millennials lagged in several responses as well. They were nearly twice as likely as adults under 30 to say society would benefit from a return to traditional gender roles. They were also the age group most likely to agree that women were taking jobs that should go to men.

I want to refrain from making some grand pronouncement about what this generational divide means. It’s entirely possible that this has nothing to do with generational differences and everything to do with the fact that the 30-44 age cohort is in the middle of having children, dividing household labor, and confronting gender roles in intensely personal ways.

It’s wonderful that we can mostly agree on equality in the abstract. The question of the 21st century is whether those principles can be translated into who takes a hit at work to figure out after-school childcare.

Top stories this week, by Maibritt Henkel

In his piece covering our new poll’s headline findings, Lakshya Jain argues that voters, despite what folks like Christopher Rufo would have you believe, don’t actually think the elite means journalists and college professors. Rather, it is billionaires and celebrities who voters suspect don’t share their values.

The Argument columnist Matt Yglesias is not convinced that American seniors are hoarding power. In his column this week, he points out that there are many real problems plaguing society, none of which have to do with old people running for office or getting tenure. Instead, we should probably be celebrating the fact that more of us are living, working, and engaging in politics for longer.

Staff writer Kelsey Piper loves a Waymo. In her latest article, she takes on a group of people who have been lobbying against the autonomous vehicles under the radar: personal injury lawyers. For the uninitiated, the musical reimagines the Orpheus-Eurydice and Hades-Persephone Greek myths in a sort of steampunk, dystopian setting. ‘It’s a sad song’ are among the first words uttered in the show, but knowing that doesn’t soften the blow.”

To this, Jeremiah added that Hadestown is an “honest tragedy,” one that “tells you directly that this has all played out before, that it's going to end badly, but that it will be beautiful anyways.”

I also recently shed a tear at the theater. Last weekend, I saw Arthur Miller’s Death of a Salesman on Broadway, starring Nathan Lane and Laurie Metcalf. Totally heart-wrenching and timeless. It made me desperately want to see the 1985 Dustin Hoffman film adaptation.

item.title: Who supports free trade? Everyone.
item.description: The populist case for economic liberalism
item.content:encoded:
By Jeremiah Johnson

Welcome back to The Argument’s poll series, where we survey Americans on the issues everyone’s fighting about. Our full crosstabs are available for paying subscribers at the end of this post. You can see every single poll published by The Argument here. Our full methodology can be read here.

Republicans used to be the party of free trade. From Gerald Ford all the way to George W. Bush, Republican presidents vocally supported lowering barriers to international commerce. Ronald Reagan said that there were no losers, only winners from trade, and the elder George Bush negotiated NAFTA while his son said that free trade helped make America into a global economic power.

Donald Trump put an end to that. Trump’s crusade to slap tariffs on an astonishingly wide range of imported goods is one of his defining policies, and economists broadly agree it’s been a disaster. One analysis showed that Trump’s tariffs increased the Consumer Price Index by 0.8 percentage points by October 2025, and a study from the Federal Reserve agreed.

Share

Economic analyses from the Tax Foundation, Penn Wharton, and the Peterson Institute all agreed that tariffs are weakening U.S. economic growth.1 The Cato Institute’s Scott Lincicome told me that adding new tariffs is like chopping off your own fingers: It’s unlikely to kill you and you can probably live a normal life afterward, but you’re causing yourself pain for no real benefit.

Though voters consistently rank cost of living as one of the most important issues facing the country, Democrats have not exactly seized the mantle of free trade.

While most rank-and-file Democrats oppose Trump’s tariffs, Joe Biden shared many of Trump’s protectionist instincts and kept many of his tariffs in place, even expanding specific tariffs on China. And prominent senators like Elizabeth Warren couched their opposition to Trump’s tariffs in terms like, “tariffs are an important strategic economic tool, but Donald Trump’s desire to start and stop random trade wars will not protect jobs.”

Prominent Democrats often seem to leave tariffs completely out of their messaging against Trump. For example, neither Kamala Harris nor Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez has tweeted the word “tariff” once this year, and Sen. Bernie Sanders has tweeted it just one time. And I used ChatGPT to scrape the congressional record for tariff mentions and analyze their sources, finding that neither AOC nor Sanders had mentioned tariffs in Congress at all this year.

Subscribe now

But, according to new polling data from The Argument, Democrats may be leaving a golden opportunity on the table. Free trade is wildly popular with Americans.

This result is consistent with other polls that asked specifically about Trump’s tariff policies. Navigator Research found that 59% have an unfavorable view of tariffs while only 29% are in favor. An ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos poll found that 64% of the public disapproved of Trump’s handling of tariffs, while a YouGov poll found that 72% think tariffs lead to higher prices. (Only 3% think they decrease prices.)

In our most recent poll of 3,000 registered voters, fielded nationally between July 20 and July 26, support for free trade was remarkably widespread. College-educated respondents supported free trade by a wider margin, but noncollege respondents overwhelmingly supported the policy as well.

In every income bracket measured, the support-to-oppose ratio was more than 4-to-1.

Free trade is popular with Republicans, Democrats, and independents. And among Democrats, it’s wildly popular with both voters who approved of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) and those who disapproved.

Free trade’s popularity is remarkably consistent across virtually every demographic and political split we measured. Indeed, our results showed that traditional economic liberalism more generally is favored by a majority of Americans — for instance, 79% of respondents opposed government ownership of most businesses, and a majority also opposed government ownership of utilities and railways.

Why did protectionism become so popular?

The intellectual climate around trade shifted dramatically after economists David Autor, David Dorn, and Gordon Hanson released their 2016 paper “The China Shock.” Their research claimed that increased trade with China led to greater job losses than economists had previously assumed and that those losses were particularly concentrated in regions with economies built around manufacturing. The findings, which showed many workers never fully recovering, shook both left and right because they appeared to confirm that globalization’s costs had been badly underestimated.

The losses from the China Shock were also concentrated in electorally important states. After Trump swept the Rust Belt states of Pennsylvania, Ohio, Wisconsin, and Michigan in 2016, many politicians concluded that free trade was electoral suicide and began embracing protectionist policy more openly. It was easy to do so by romanticizing manufacturing jobs as “Real America,” the type of honest work that carried more cultural legitimacy than white-collar or service-industry jobs.

But the lessons from the China Shock were overlearned. More recent research has called into question the scale of the shock. One paper from Lorenzo Caliendo, Maximiliano Dvorkin, and Fernando Parro found that only 16% of the decline in manufacturing employment from 2000 to 2007 could be traced back to the China Shock, while other research emphasized that when you examine all employment sectors, increased trade with China may have led to net job gains.

Subscribe now

And even the authors of the original paper emphasized that their findings were primarily focused around local shocks and didn’t dispute the overall benefits of free trade. The New York Times reported that David Autor, “like most economists, is still persuaded of the long-established benefits that global trade confers on the economy as a whole.” He believes the benefits are large and widespread but diffuse, while the losses are painfully concentrated.

The authors are also deeply skeptical that more tariffs can fix any of this. Gordon Hanson wrote that “China’s rise, although disruptive for many workers, has nevertheless benefited the U.S. economy” and rejected protectionism, instead calling on the U.S. to rejoin the Trans-Pacific Partnership. Trump’s barrage of new tariffs in his second term has not led to a manufacturing renaissance, with the U.S. continuing to lose manufacturing jobs since he took office.

Importantly, the political momentum that led to increased support for protectionism has stopped. Trump’s use of tariffs has been so lawless, so haphazardly implemented, and so offensive to so many of America’s traditional allies that the public has clearly turned against tariffs and back toward free trade.

Of course, it’s entirely plausible that voters approve of free trade in the abstract while specific trade liberalization deals, with all their inherent messiness, are more likely to attract disapproval (especially once interest groups, such as particular unions that benefit from the status quo, get to have their say).

But the good news is that Democrats don’t have to negotiate a new NAFTA or a new Trans-Pacific Partnership to champion free trade. They can just promise to undo Trump’s newest tariffs with a stroke of the pen when they retake the presidency.

If free trade is so popular, what’s stopping Democrats from attacking Republicans more vigorously on the issue?

One theory is that Democrats are worried about losing support from unions and other interest groups that have a vested interest in tariffs. But capitulating to unions on protectionist policy isn’t working.

Joe Biden was the most pro-union president in generations. The American Rescue Plan bailed out the Teamsters union — providing approximately $35.8 billion to keep the Central States pension plan solvent and protecting over 350,000 participants from benefit reductions of roughly 60% — and the Teamsters still didn’t endorse Biden or Harris in 2024.

Democrats may simply be so used to catering to unions that it’s hard to break the pattern. But the time will never be better to overcome the old protectionist muscle memory and come out forcefully for free trade.

But each still reached the same conclusion, broadly.

item.title: #MeToo didn’t go far enough
item.description: Can women ever be free from fear?
item.content:encoded:
By Jerusalem Demsas

Once a month, Matt and I do a book club episode of The Argument podcast. In an upcoming episode this month, we are reading Bowling Alone by Robert Putnam. Read along if you are interested, and please comment with any questions or ideas you would like us to explore!

True freedom requires a person with a will — and a society that is organized to allow the expression of that will.

I can want something as simple as to walk my dog at night. But if roving gangs threaten my life, then my freedom to pursue that desire is only theoretical. Even worse is if the threat is so pervasive that I can’t even imagine walking my dog at night. In neither case am I really free.

This diminished freedom has long been, to greater and lesser degrees, the status quo for most women in most places.

Share

Even in a society as egalitarian as the contemporary U.S., polling shows that women feel less safe to roam. Globally, “men are over 20% more likely than women to say they feel safe in their communities.” One paper about women in Delhi finds that women will choose to go to much worse colleges in order to feel safer while traveling, whereas men with similar choices will choose to attend the better colleges more frequently.

One researcher, Alice Evans, recently argued that “our analyses of progress towards gender equality still focus on economic activity and political representation, omitting a far more basic question: can women walk down the street alone at night and be at ease?”

It is not immediately obvious that women should feel less free than men: Men are much more likely than women to be victims of homicide and robbery. Of course, a big part of this is that boys are more likely to be in public spaces unsupervised in the first place.

The freedom to move in the world unburdened by the fear of violence and harassment is a fundamental prerequisite to basically every other freedom we care about: to say what you really think, to associate with whomever you wish. It can be hard to imagine a world where the average woman remains physically weaker than the average man and yet feels as free. But one thing gives me hope: If you were to describe the freedom enjoyed by many women in rich, low-crime neighborhoods in modern-day America to a woman living in the 1700s, it would become clear just how much legal, social, and cultural progress can be made.

#MeToo’s unfinished revolution

The slogan Me Too was first used in 2006 by the activist Tarana Burke to promote what she called “empowerment through empathy.” The idea was that victims of sexual violence and harassment often feel isolated by their experiences. Making people aware that there are others who have gone through the same thing plausibly makes them feel less alone.

But after the hashtag went truly viral in 2017, the slogan’s original purpose no longer seemed to meet the enormity of the task. The allegations against Harvey Weinstein and other abusive male power brokers were horrifying, and the veritable downpour of crimes revealed by women everywhere felt endless. We couldn’t wait for the broad social awareness being cultivated by the hashtag to trickle down into people’s behavior. Responding to stories of assault, harassment, and inequality with mere “likes” on social media was clearly not enough.

But the signal failure of #MeToo was that in seeking to counteract the norm of doubting women’s accounts, “accused” became nearly synonymous with “guilty.” More broadly, #MeToo, by highlighting women’s vulnerability, cast all men in the role of perpetrator.

Subscribe now

In 2022, Burke wrote a retrospective in which she gave examples of the accomplishments of #MeToo. Besides removing “captains of industry” from positions of power, her examples were largely expressive:

  • “More than any law that has been passed or policy that has been changed in the past five years, this movement has created visibility and community.”

  • “The language we use is shifting, replacing words like victim with survivor.”

  • “We talk about mental health and healing.”

  • “[E]mployers are crafting thoughtful human-resource policies.”

  • “Consumers are more conscientious about the cultural content they consume.”

  • Consumers are “vocal about calling out rape culture.”

Burke, not totally comfortable with this accounting, quoted another feminist author, Imani Perry, who argued that “awareness is not a virtue in and of itself.” Burke expressed ambivalence about incarcerating more rapists and ended her piece by calling on the reader to do their part.

But what is their part? If awareness is not enough, and the goal is to effect mass cultural change without incarcerating a lot more rapists, what exactly should we be doing?

My cohost Matt Yglesias argued that the #MeToo movement was thin on specific demands and failed to accomplish very much, which is reasonable enough. Earlier feminist wins were concrete: Recognize our right to vote. Recognize our right to own property. Recognize our right to divorce our husbands and attend college.

The main problem is that both critics and supporters of the #MeToo movement tended to underrate just how radically society would have to change for women to feel as safe as men, or even to come close.

For starters, there is no specific legislative demand that could eliminate sexual harassment. And sexual violence is different from other serious crimes like murder or theft. There is often not dispositive physical evidence like there would be if someone shot you or broke into your house, and therefore cases are typically based almost entirely on witness testimony.

Moreover, victims themselves are often torn about going through the legal system. Sometimes they just want to move on rather than deal with a years-long process that may retraumatize them while hinging entirely on their perceived credibility as a witness. Sometimes the perpetrator is a friend, partner, or community member who they don’t actually want sent to jail.

And, of course, so much of what makes women and girls feel unsafe is not rape itself but the threat of sexual harassment that does not rise to the level of criminal activity.

True equality for women cannot exist in a world where girls are afraid to walk home from school alone and women have to remain on high alert while going about their normal lives. The unfortunate fact is that you can’t legislate freedom.

You can’t bar men from catcalling 13-year-olds, or from leering at women jogging at night. So, what do you do? I don’t think there’s an obvious answer.

item.title: Pigs vs. democracy
item.content:encoded:
By John Robert Thomason

Welcome to The Closing Argument, our verdict on the news, plus everything The Argument published and appeared in this week.

The Verdict, by John Thomason

Americans, we keep learning, are obsessed with the price of groceries. At the same time, many of them seem very uncomfortable with one of the ways that meat producers make groceries cheap: by cramming livestock so close together that they can’t even turn around.

When you pose this problem to voters a kind of commonsense decency can sometimes win out: Healthy majorities in Florida, Arizona, Massachusetts, and California have voted in favor of raising confinement standards over the last 25 years.

You might notice that none of those are major pork-producing states.

But because the initiatives in California and Massachusetts limited not just what their farmers could do, but also what sorts of animal products could be sold within their borders at all, the animal welfare implications were immense, amounting to perhaps the most substantial protections for farmed animals in U.S. history. The 2018 passage of California’s Proposition 12 meant that, if hog farmers in Iowa want to sell whole cuts of pork to Californians (which they very much do), they have to abide by Golden State standards.

All of that was almost thrown out over the course of this spring and summer.

The Farm Bill is a sprawling document that covers everything from food stamps to irrigation programs — an ideal vehicle for a policy change to escape public notice. That seems to be at least in part what the proponents of the Save Our Bacon Act were hoping for. The provision, championed by members of Iowa’s congressional delegation, would have preempted state-level reforms like California’s and Massachusetts’s, making it impossible for states to bar the sale of pork from pigs whose mothers couldn’t turn around or extend their limbs during pregnancy (so long as those farms’ states allow it).

Farm-state Republicans lined up behind the provision, while food safety groups, animal rights groups, and most of the Democratic Senate caucus were against it. (The pork industry is actually split between those who have not yet complied with strict standards and those who have already invested in compliant practices.) The latter appeared to be winning out in June, when the Senate decided not to include the provision, apparently over the controversy it had engendered. But that doesn’t mean Save Our Bacon is dead. The Farm Bill stalled in the Senate Agriculture Committee on Thursday, over a dispute on an entirely different issue, with the committee now in recess until the fall. The Save Our Bacon Act is likely to get a second wind at that time.

If we’re being honest, the vast majority of the nation didn’t just miss this drama — they probably wouldn’t have cared all that much if they’d known.

It’s common to hear political junkies talk about “high salience” and “low salience” issues. The cost of pork is high salience — something voters will definitely notice and express their dissatisfaction about at the polls — while the welfare of the pigs who suffered to keep prices down is low salience, the purview largely of those who in some sense have made a choice to care about it.

With high salience issues, the will of the voters is clear enough and the cost of ignoring it is losing elections. But on low salience issues, democracies count on elite political actors reaching some sort of reasonable agreement that is in the best interests of the public.

The conflict over Save Our Bacon unsettles the idea that low and high salience issues are cleanly separable.

First of all, which “will of the voters” should be honored in this situation? That of the median 2024 voter, angry about the price of groceries, or those of the actual majorities in multiple states who voted for farm animal protections? (Even Iowa voters appear to reject the Save Our Bacon Act, though the poll in question was commissioned by an advocacy organization.)

Still, asking people to improve pigs’ lives is one thing; asking them to pay a lot more for bacon, let alone give it up entirely, is another. Ending farm animal suffering would require the latter. If animal rights become high salience, animal rights groups lose. If it stays low salience, then they never even get a shot at winning. Such is the fate of those with unpopular convictions in a democratic society.

No country for moral fanatics?

Four years ago, a very small dog wandered into my life, and it changed my politics forever.

I had always been a little judgy about people who dote on their pets, yet there I was, realizing that I might find myself in tears if this ornery creature had so much as a hangnail. It no longer made sense to me to care so much about the welfare of this one animal without caring about others who seemed just like him.

Most market hogs are mutilated without anesthesia, spend their lives on bare slats above their own manure, and never go outdoors until slaughter. If we did any of this to dogs we’d call it torture. None of this was exactly news to me, I’m ashamed to say, but for the first time I actually felt that it might be impossible to live with myself if I knew that, while I doted on this dog, creatures just like him were being put through hell on earth for me.

In a political climate where we’re constantly being told that the moral stakes are higher than ever — that, as former President Obama lamented in 2015, “those who disagree with us are not merely wrong but bad” — contemplating the fate of livestock induces a kind of vertiginous loneliness, precisely because it’s not a matter of public controversy. Quite the opposite: Per-capita meat consumption has never been higher, and all either party can talk about is making that consumption cheaper. Meanwhile, more than 80 billion farm animals are slaughtered worldwide every year after the sort of lives I described above.

But different people have dramatically different moral red lines. Many of my fellow citizens think that we’re living through a genocide of unborn children. Others think that we should strip private property rights from anyone with one too many 0’s in their net worth. I don’t agree with either of them, and most of them don’t agree with me. We have to live together anyway. A certain amount of moral loneliness — the kind that could keep you up at night, aghast at the evil that people will tolerate — is the price that every zealot pays to live in a democratic society. At least I know they won’t hang me for it.

It’s uncomfortable to realize you’re part of a moral minority. What options do you have, besides the despair of accepting majority will, or the tireless fanaticism that characterizes groups like PETA?

It’s here that I take some solace in the weird indeterminacy of representative democracy. If you put the actual question I care about before voters — would you give up meat as you know it to end farm animal suffering? — it would lose. If you put the question purely to elite power brokers, it would also lose.

In a majoritarian society, moral minorities will never be entirely satisfied. Ninety-nine percent of the time this brings me great relief: I don’t want anti-abortion zealots dictating health policy by fiat. Yet I too believe that egregious moral crimes are being committed daily and, yes, I would impose my preference for stopping these crimes on everyone else if I could. If only I could.

But of course I don’t want to be imposed upon myself. For all its backsliding, the American system still does a pretty good job of ensuring that. And the very fragmentation that helps shore up this freedom — the separation of powers, the strategic veto points, the uneasy coalitions — also gives radicals of every stripe avenues to pursue their goals. It’s not such a lonely place for a fanatic after all.
